steps: Write down the oven settings: 425F, 25 minutes.
Lower the temperature: 425 minus 25 is 400F, and the time stays 25 minutes.
Or shorten the time: 25 × 0.75 = 18.75, rounded to 19 minutes, at the same 425F.

parts.meaning: The air fryer runs hotter than the dial says, because the fan pushes hot air straight onto the food. Dropping 25F keeps the edges from burning before the centres soften.
When you lower the temperature, the food still needs the full oven time. The lower heat and the full time balance each other out.
A quarter sooner. Keep the oven temperature and check at three quarters of the oven time. Open the basket then and look for browned edges.

formula.text: Pick one, never both. Lower the temperature: air fryer temp = oven temp minus 25F, and the time stays the same. Or shorten the time: keep the oven temperature and check at oven time × 0.75. For vegetables at 425F for 25 minutes: either 400F for 25 minutes, or 425F and check at about 19 minutes.

howToSteps.name: Read the oven settings
howToSteps.text: Find the temperature and time in your recipe. Roast vegetables usually bake at 425F for 25 minutes.

howToSteps.name: Pick one change
howToSteps.text: Pick one change, not both. Either take 25F off the temperature and keep the time, or keep the temperature and check a quarter sooner. 425F for 25 minutes becomes either 400F for 25 minutes or 425F and check at about 19 minutes.

howToSteps.name: Cut evenly and toss in oil
howToSteps.text: Cut the vegetables to a similar size and toss with a teaspoon of oil and seasoning.

howToSteps.name: Cook, shake, and check
howToSteps.text: Spread in a single layer and shake twice. Pull them when the edges brown.

title: Oven to Air Fryer: Roast Vegetables
tutorial: Vegetables are where the air fryer earns its place on a weeknight. A tray of vegetables that roasts at 425F for 25 minutes air fries two ways: 400F for the full 25 minutes, or 425F and check at about 19 minutes. Either way the edges brown more, and the waiting is shorter.

The oil is not optional. Toss the vegetables in a teaspoon of oil before they go in, because dry vegetables go leathery instead of crisp. The oil carries the heat into the surface and helps it brown. One teaspoon is enough for a full basket.

Cut them the same size, and cut them for the vegetable. Dense vegetables like carrots and butternut squash need small pieces, about half an inch, or the outside burns before the centre softens. Quick vegetables like asparagus and green beans can stay whole. Even pieces cook evenly, and even cooking is the whole point of the conversion.

Shake twice, not once. Vegetables shrink as they cook, and the pieces that start on top end up buried. Shake at the halfway mark and again near the end, and every piece gets its turn at the top where the heat is strongest.

Dense vegetables take longer than the converted time sometimes, and thin ones finish sooner. Beets and whole squash are the slowest cooks in the basket. Asparagus and mushrooms are the fastest. Check about a quarter sooner, look, and decide then.
